1.75.m: Vyāsa said: / Having heard the word of Maheśvara, the gods headed by Śakra / rushed from all sides against those hosts of Daityas, all against all.
The mighty-armed great Asura named Kumbha came forward; / the Nairṛta struck the king of the Yakṣas fiercely with a mace.
The lord of the Guhyakas struck the foremost [Asura] violently with strokes of his mace; / then a terrible mace-duel took place between the two,
with circular entanglements, great grappling, pinning from the front to slay, / extensive, frightful movement, bursting and shattering blows.
Having fought a great battle with him, at the end the lord of wealth / brought down a bursting blow upon the chest of that Kumbha.
Then Kumbha, with shattered tusks, fell upon the surface of the earth. / Standing on his chariot, the exceedingly heroic Jambha then struck Harihaya
with heaps of arrows, and likewise Airāvaṇa vehemently. / Vāsava pierced the foremost Asura with his thunderbolt.
He fell upon the surface of the earth, lifeless and smeared with blood. / Likewise, Araṇya, Sughora, Aghora, and Ghora—
four troop leaders he pierced in battle with his spear; / and the commander of the army brought them each down with agility.
Jayanta subdued Saurabha with showers of arrows; / and Saṃhrāda, weapon in hand, Yamadaṇḍa, and Narāntaka,
having slain, he felled, their bodies reduced to ashes. / And Kāla felled Bābhrava with a stroke of his sword;
Mṛtyu pierced Aśva and Nirghṛṇaka with his spear in battle; / and these seven exceedingly mighty ones were consumed by Agni.
Bhadrabāhu, Mahābāhu, Sugaṃdha, and Gaṃdha, / Bhaurika, Vallika, and Bhīma—these were the commanders marching at the head of the army.
Their bodies completely consumed by fire in battle, they fell dead upon the earth. / Bound by the nooses of high-souled Varuṇa, those mighty heroes
of great strength, fearsome even to brave men, fell to the ground. / Five Dānavas were slain by the net of rays of the sun-god [or: the hero's blazing rays]:
Turu, Tuṃburu, Durmedhas, Sādhaka, and the one named Asādhaka, / Krūra, Krauñca, Raṇeśāna, Moda, Saṃmoda, and the six-faced [daityas].
The Daityas were brought down in combat by the wind-god with his arrows; / the lord of the Nairṛtas struck down Bhīma to the earth with his club.
And by the trident strikes of the Rudras, Daityas and Dānavas by the hundreds, / facing them in front, skilled in battle, fell down terrified in the conflict.
By the showers of arrows from the Vasus and the heroic, ray-garlanded [Ādityas], / and by the hail of clouds, and terrible lightning strikes,
the mighty Daityas were brought down by the hundreds in battle; / they fell by thousands beneath the blows of Kubera's club.
The foremost Daityas were pierced by Indra's thunderbolt itself; / countless numbers fell to the earth, struck down likewise by Skanda's spear.
The most prominent leaders fell beneath the stroke of Gaṇeśa's axe. / By the discus of fierce action loosed from Vaikuṇṭha's hand,
the heads of the eminent Daityas fell upon the ground. / Yama, the destroyer, with his rod of chastisement, struck down by tens of millions and thousands
the Dānavas upon the earth, while Kāla [struck them down] with his sword, / Mṛtyu with his spear, and the Noose-Wielder [Varuṇa] others with his noose.
By the descent of Takṣaka and other serpents, and by the coldness of the moon, / the cavalry, donkeys, horses, elephants, and many others were overcome with the noose.
Then, with an iron club striking the frontal globes of their elephants, he destroyed the Daityas; / thus with lightness of hand did he bring down the horses and elephants.
In this manner, by the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Apsarases of great might, / and by other deities along with the leaders of the troop of Mothers,
those most dreadful Dānavas of dissolution were struck down / with arrows, sword-blows, spears, javelins, and battle-axes.
With staffs, iron clubs, and lances, the gods struck down the Asuras. / While they were being thus decimated, the king of the Daityas stepped forward.
Resembling the chariot of the sun, adorned with jewel-like chariots, / made of gold, divine, bedecked with bells and chowries,
filled with pennons and banners, charming, resembling the chariot of Indra— / mounting this, the greatly heroic Hiraṇyākṣa, lord of the Asuras,
irresistible to gods and Asuras, attacked with volleys of arrows. / The hero brought down to the earth armies, elephants,
and chariots together with their swift horses, by the hundreds and by the thousands. / Thus roaming amid all the hosts of heaven's dwellers,
the lord of the Daityas showered streams of arrows resembling death itself. / And then in due order in that battle he churned the armies of the gods,
just as an elephant [churns] a lotus thicket in a cluster of ponds, / with sharp arrow-strikes, with swift speed, and with lion-roars again and again.
Then with great speed they fell upon the earth before that lord of Daityas; / he struck Jayanta with ten exceedingly sharp-pointed arrows.
He struck Revanta with five arrows, Indra with fifteen, / Citraratha with twenty, Guha with twenty-five,
Heramba with three arrows, and Yama with forty arrows; / likewise Kāla and Mṛtyu with double that hand-count [eighty arrows];
the lord of the Guhyakas [Kubera] and the Life-Breath of the World [Vāyu] each with ten arrows; / all the Rudras separately with six and seven arrows each;
and all the Vasus, Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Pannagas with arrows; / with ten, eighteen, and six arrows did he pierce the gods in the battle.
Because of his flood of vigor, his immense prowess, and the display of his swift dexterity, / the gods, having fallen into peril, were unable to retaliate out of fear.
Struck in the battle with vital-point-piercing arrows resembling Maheśa's trident, / the gods swooned and fell to the ground.
The foremost gods were unable even to stand before his face. / Then the gods, shattered and put to flight together with the lord of the third heaven [Indra],
being sorely afflicted, went for refuge to Hari, the refuge of all. / In the meantime, Viṣṇu spoke to victorious Garuḍa, the lord of birds:
"Go now before the face of the Daitya at the head of the battle / for his destruction!" Thereupon he swiftly went into his presence with speed.
Piercing the chariot with his arrows, [the Daitya] blocked the speed of Viṣṇu. / Facing the chariot, the Daitya spoke to the imperishable Viṣṇu:
"Today, having slain you along with the gods, I will create another creation!" / Then Viṣṇu spoke these words to the roaring, foremost of Daityas:
"You are capable of boasting, O wicked one; stand firm in battle if you can!" / Thereupon [the Daitya] struck the imperishable Viṣṇu with hundreds of arrows.
Unflinching, [Viṣṇu] cut down those arrows that resembled Yama's rod. / Again [the Daitya] discharged thousands of arrows at him in battle.
Slicing through them with his arrows, Śauri pierced him in turn with shafts / that appeared immovable through their immense weight, like submarine fires to the touch,
piercing, sharp, soaring through the sky, and swift as thought. / By the dexterity of Keśava's weapon, which rendered [his defenses] like dry blades of grass and cotton,
the foremost Daitya, struck by thousands of golden shafts, / was afflicted with pain; enraged, he seized a mountain in the battle
and with great force the mighty Hiraṇyākṣa hurled it at Mādhava. / But Hari playfully pulverized it to powder with his mace.
In this very way, a thousand mountains were hurled in succession, / and in that same way, with ease, they were crushed to dust by Hari, the foe of the Dānavas.
Then, producing a thousand arms, that best of Dānavas / with his mind possessed by wrath showered Viṣṇu with arrows,
fierce spears, tridents, battle-axes, and many other weapons. / But the best of the gods severed all those hurled by him
with blazing, terrible arrows that terrified the Asuras; / with arrows resembling Śambhu's trident, he pierced all his limbs.
Thus the lord of the Dānavas [fought] in battle against the imperishable Lord Hari. / And succumbing to fury, he hurled his unsurpassed spear of all-power,
dreadful as the tongue of Kāla, furnished with eight bells; / rushing forward, he swiftly cast it against Hari's broad chest.
That best of gods shone like a dense cloud illuminated by lightning. / Then the Daityas cried aloud in joy, shouting, "Victory! Well done!"
Then Hari, the foe of the Dānavas, loosed his discus into the Daitya army; / having severed their heads, it returned once again to Mādhava.
He felled that Daitya with the stroke of his spear in battle. / Regaining consciousness after a long time, [the Daitya], enraged, struck Keśava
with a fire arrow; Hari cast the weapon of Kubera against him. / Then [the Daitya] loosed a magical Asura weapon of exceedingly terrible power:
lions, tigers, buffaloes, as well as elephants and serpents— / with these the valorous Hiraṇyākṣa attacked Viṣṇu in battle.
Then Hari severed with his arrows the floods of arms and weapons born of the magical weapon in battle, / and struck [the Daitya] with his trident.
With all his limbs paralyzed, instantly drenched in blood, / his body bathed in gore, [the Daitya] was dragged away by Viṣṇu as he destroyed him.
The lord of gods pierced that trident with three arrows, / and with ten arrows Hari cut down the chariot body with its standard, flag, chariot, parasol,
and the charioteer. / When the chariot was felled, the Daitya leaped up and then mounted another chariot,
that mighty lord of Daityas, and faced [him]. / Then a battle took place, exceedingly fierce, causing the hair to stand on end,
astonishing the worlds, a great clash between Hiraṇyākṣa and Hari, / a battle of divine weapons, an exchange of blow and counter-blow.
Then, in close combat, a full hundred celestial years passed. / Thereupon the Daitya of immense prowess grew in size like Vāmana.
In anger he seized with his mouth the three worlds with the moving and unmoving; / lifting up the orb of the earth, he entered Rasātala.
And the remaining Daityas entered after him, filled with delight. / Then Viṣṇu of great splendour, realizing the great might of the Daitya,
assumed the form of a boar, wishing to slay the king of Daityas. / Taking on the body of a boar, Viṣṇu entered swiftly after him.
Having gone there to the base of the earth, seeing the earth fallen into Rasātala, / he lifted upon his two tusks the earth, the support of the worlds.
As Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendour was going bearing her, / the lord of Daityas came forward, boldly goading him with words.
Viṣṇu, whose form was an illusory boar, enduring the harsh words in anger, / placed this earth, as the supporter of the earth, upon the water.
Infusing his own strength into her, he then made her firm. / Afterward the king of Daityas, closely pursuing, drew near.
Overcome by great rage, he struck Hari with a mace. / Viṣṇu as the boar by his illusory power dodged that mace,
as one endowed with yoga avoids death, and struck him with Kaumodakī. / Then, overcome with rage again, the mighty Hiraṇyākṣa
struck the lord, the god, with his fist upon the right arm. / Thus a very fierce battle ensued, moving left and right, back and forth,
with whirling, casting, and tit-for-tat actions. / Then the gods headed by Brahmā, standing in the sky, watching the battle,
said, "May there be well-being for the creatures, the gods, and the sages!" / And they said to Viṣṇu, the god of gods, in the form of a boar:
"O God, do not play like a child! Slay this thorn in the side of the gods!" / Thereupon Viṣṇu of great splendour, bearing the form of the illusory boar,
obtaining the approval of Brahmā and the others, cast his terrible discus, / resembling a thousand suns, with a thousand spokes, of great brilliance,
bringing destruction to the Daityas, dreadful, resembling the fire of cosmic dissolution. / That discus discharged by Viṣṇu reduced the mighty Hiraṇyākṣa
instantly to ashes before the eyes of Brahmā and the others. / And the dreadful discus, the destroyer of the Daityas, returned to Acyuta.
Then the gods headed by Brahmā, and the guardians of the world headed by Śakra, / seeing the victory of Viṣṇu, assembled and praised him.

The gods said: / "We bow down to Viṣṇu, the primal origin of the universe, the lord of gods and asuras, the guardian of the worlds, / from whose navel lotus the lotus-born [Brahmā] arose; to him indeed we have gone for refuge.
Homage, homage to the bearer of the fish form! Homage to you who bear the tortoise form! / We bow to the one in the form of a man-lion, and again homage to the one in the form of a dwarf!

Homage to you, Rāma, the destroyer of the Kṣatriyas! To Rāma, the destroyer of the ten-faced [Rāvaṇa]! / Homage to the slayer of Pralamba, clad in dark blue! Homage to the Buddha, the deluder of the Daityas!

And to the one named Kalkin, the destroyer of the barbarians! Homage again to the bearer of the boar's form! / For the welfare of the world, cosmic age after cosmic age, you assume a form for the destruction of the asuras.
Indeed, just now by you was slaughtered this insolent Daitya named Hiraṇyākṣa, / who in mere sport humiliated the world-guardians headed by Indra.
He was indeed struck down by you for the sake of the gods' welfare. O best of gods, be gracious! / You are the creator of this universe in the form of Brahmā, O God of gods!
You alone are its protector, and cosmic age after cosmic age you assume delightful forms; / and becoming Hara, the fire of time, you will bring the universe to destruction at the time of the end.
Therefore you alone are the cause of the universe; beyond you there is nothing living or non-living, O Lord. / Whatever has been, whatever has the form of the future, and likewise what is present—
you alone are all that is called moving and unmoving; no universe shines without you. / The nature of being and non-being, grounded in the distinction of 'it is' and 'it is not,' shines in you alone.
Therefore no one of unripened intellect is capable of knowing you, O God, / except for a person devoted to your feet; therefore we have come to you for refuge, who are worthy of refuge."
Vyāsa said: / Then Viṣṇu, his heart delighted, said to the dwellers in heaven: / "I am pleased, O gods, with your praise now. May good fortune be yours!
Whoever recites this hymn of victory with devotion and reverence, / nothing in the three worlds is difficult for him to attain, O gods.
Whatever fruit is attained from giving a hundred thousand cows properly, / that fruit a man attains from reciting or hearing [it].
The praise of the God of gods constantly grants all desires. / Beyond this, no great knowledge has been or ever will be."

1.76.m: Saṃjaya said: / "Those asuras who died in the battle facing forward or turned away— / I wish to hear truly of their destiny, O holy man.
Innumerable are these Daityas in the three worlds, among the moving and unmoving. / Even today, where have they gone? Tell me this, O master!"
Vyāsa said: / "Those heroes who died facing forward in the battle, the foremost of the Daityas, / having attained godhood themselves, enjoy eternal enjoyment,
where there are golden palaces adorned with various gems, / trees that grant all desires, possessing water from the celestial river,
and an auspicious pond filled with lotuses, blue water-lilies, fragrant white water-lilies and other flowers, / and with curds, milk, ghee, and candied sugar.
Endowed with immense beauty, ever possessing fresh youth, / they rule a kingdom there, and likewise on the surface of the earth.
Thus having attained eight births as wealthy men, superintendents, and ministers, / with their bodies partially facing forward, they enjoy heaven eternally.
Those who turned away, cowards, fearful, and those who used deceit in battle, / they go to a dreadful hell, as do those who hate gods and twice-born.
Those who slay a warrior in battle who has fallen, fainted, broken down, or is fighting another, / go to hell; and they become barbarians speaking foul words.
Those who steal the deposits of others are indeed those who turned their backs; / or thieves who act rashly at night or when lost in a forest;
fools given to eating anything, barbarians, slayers of cows and Brahmins, / foul-speaking other barbarians, and those who are of low birth.
Their speech is demoniacal; for them there is no worldly conduct; / there is no purity, asceticism, knowledge, nor libations to gods and ancestors,
nor gift-giving, ancestral rites, and the like in sacrifice, nor worship of the gods; / nor service to ancestors, the twice-born, deities, and ascetics.
Due to the absence of knowledge, they have no cleansing of excrement; / and they lust after mother, sister, and another's wife."
Everything has become inverted from the world; good conduct has become defiled. / Among the descendants of Tārkṣya, the Vatsas, and other lineage-dwellers,
daityas are continually born in the family, for whom merit is of no account. / When dead, those slayers of twice-born, women, and infants go to an evil state.
Those evil-minded consumers of beef, intent on eating uneatable food— / they go to the womb of an insect, or become trees and ants.
Those enemies of the gods are fit neither for mantras nor for the gods; / their elder brother is their equal, and they follow vulgar ways of life.
Plucking body-hair and head-hair, intent on eating raw flesh on earth, / [taking part in] violence, vow, gift, bathing, sacrifice, and the like—
taking pleasure in fish, meat, and the like, speaking false words, / always lustful, always greedy, always filled with anger and arrogance,
delighting in killing and binding, agitated, fond of gambling and music, / served by bad servants, delighting in wicked folk, men fond of foul smells,
having no resolve concerning the gods, the wise, or the hearing of dharma, / or concerning holy hymns, mantras, and their proper tasks—
possessing many diseases and great wrath, having many forms and possessions: / these are the marks of the daityas among human births on earth.
They know neither the other world nor a teacher, neither their own nor another; / they desire only to fill their belly, caring nothing for guest, teachers, or twice-born,
nor for a deity, a son, lineage, friend, or kinsman. / Even in a dream they do not understand gift-giving, food, nourishment, or attire.
Since they hoard wealth, they are yakṣas in human form; / even at the moment of death they give away no wealth, O king.
Those yakṣas dwell in an evil state, carriers of burdens for the sake of others. / Or consider the mark of pretas, which is despised by all the world,
among women and men; hear it with one mind from me: / Constantly bearing filth and mud, devoid of truth and purity,
with heaps of dirt on their teeth, hair, clothes, and body, / the cleansing of house, seat, and vessels never pleases them even once.
They do not see the happiness of women; they quickly enter the forest; / intent upon the eating of leftover scraps, leavings, and rotting food on earth,
eating, drinking, and sleeping in darkness pleases them; / at no time is there wellness, nor any cleanliness on their body.
Such indeed is the mark of pretas in the human realms: / they know neither benefit nor harm, friend nor enemy, virtue nor vice,
sin, merit, and the like, sacred place, bathing, or worship of gods and twice-born; / by their very nature they distinguish neither enemy, friend, nor neutral.
Those abiding in mortal form are beasts, known as such by those of discerning intellect; / by their intellect they have diverse dispositions, and wander falsely upon the earth.
Those men in the form of yakṣas are excluded from all rites; / I shall declare their division and characteristics on the surface of the earth.
Born in the mortal realms according to their very sins: / one who stands on foul ground, an urbanite of deceitful form,
eating remnants and scraps—the wise call such a one a crow. / An evil one intent on uneatable food, fond of putrid smells, is a dog.
Engaged in all household [vices], living on both proper and improper food, / they take their birth on earth in the families of beasts and other wombs.
Taking a dog in hand, they are mlecchas, fond of eating [it], / especially pigs and also fighting cocks.
Fond of rearing and eating [them], fond of putrid and wretched, base things, / making fire upon a mountain, gathering stores of wood—
they are to be known always as mlecchas, filled with fear of kṣatriyas. / When the dharma of the people is destroyed, and always devoid of purity,
then the well-born will become mlecchas and robbers. / From association with them, through kinship and eating their food,
and through intercourse with their women, they attain their very condition. / At that time, all people will be tormented by misery and disease,
deluded in their pursuit of food during famine, constantly oppressed by the king. / There mortals will be devoted to falsehood, devoid of all purity.
The Purāṇas, Āgamas, and Saṃhitās are not heard by the people at all; / fond of liquor and meat, evil, omnivorous, exceedingly cruel,
intent on dreadful conduct, always devoted to deceit, / sons do not support their father, their mother, or their elders.
Servants do not attend upon a virtuous master; / some women do not serve their husband, parents-in-law, or their own mothers.
Men there are in perpetual misery, and there is strife in every house; / the kings are mlecchas and wine-drinkers, and so are the ministers and royal priests.
Their offerings are made with human beings, with fish, and with meats, without fleshless offerings; / owing to the practices of heretics, they take the lead in gossip and [worldly] talk.
The surface of the earth is covered by the rich, by cuckoos, and by dullards; / thereafter, deluded people, mutual lovers in the forest or in towns,
men eat both edible and inedible food, fish, meat, and the like; / and other twice-born in the forest eat whatever is sinful.
The devoted, the beast, and any other—all go to non-rebirth; / all those evil ones, formerly gods, cast down the ancestors.
Piśācas, rākṣasas, mortals, and guhyakas surely— / these, delighting in indiscipline, are neither gods nor humans.
Saṃjaya said: / And how do the knowers of truth recognize these marks in mortal states? / Dispel this doubt of mine on that point, O lord.
Vyāsa said: / Corresponding to the sins they committed, among twice-born and other castes, / asuras, rākṣasas, and pretas do not abandon their innate nature.
Those asuras born as mortals are always eager for conflict; / deceitful, foul, and cruel—they are to be known as rākṣasas on earth.
Gift-giving that causes distress to people, and likewise worship of gods on earth— / having gained wealth through fierce disposition, they enjoy everlasting kingship.
Victory, valor, and the like, which are merits, turn again to the destruction of sin; / thus on earth, as in heaven, in the realm of the nāgas, and in the abode of Yama.
By severe austerity someone attains divine status in heaven; / having worshipped Vāsudeva, Prahlāda was revered by the gods.
Likewise, the daitya Andhaka, having praised Hara, became a member of his assembly; / the mighty Bhṛṅgin attained leadership of his gaṇas.
These and many others—Bali will become Indra— / they attain a good destination, dear one, here and in the hereafter always.
Some born in the family of the daityas are the best among the gods on earth; / they uplift all the ancestors by hundreds and by thousands.
Even by a single wise son, the deliverance of the family is achieved; / even a single Vaiṣṇava son can redeem ten million [generations of] family.
Even one with subdued senses, righteous, devoted to worshipping twice-born and gods— / when dharma decays at the end of the Kali age, in city and countryside,
a single righteous person protects the city, village, people, and family. / There was a great city of brāhmaṇas, rich with learned men.
There all the twice-born were constantly devoted to the twilight worship, / steadfast, intent on the recitation of the Veda, worshippers of gods, guests, and twice-born,
performing sacrifices, vows, and fire rituals, firmly settled in the six duties; / even in extreme distress, their mind never turned toward sin.
Courageously they constantly performed the eternal vows and sacrifices. / Once, by the turn of fate, a wise householder,
The brahmin sage, knower of mantras, pours clarified butter into the fire with a mantra; / and at that time there arose for him a very severe difficulty in urination.
He went to discharge it, having placed a servant-girl for guard; / but through her inattention, a dog ate the ghee.
Out of fear, she then filled the vessel with her own urine. / Without noticing, that vipra in haste then offered it into the fire.
A marvel was then instantly observed by him in the fire: / a solid mass of gold, indeed real gold shining like Jāmbūnada gold.
Taking it with joy, the vipra engaged in a sinful course. / In astonishment he asked the servant-girl: "Tell me, my dear, how did this happen?"
With joy she told him what had happened, O dvija. / From then on, daily at the proper time, that practice went on for him.
There was wondrous prosperity in the house, causing astonishment among the people. / Then, having heard about it from one another, in that city everyone
having heard of it, the wicked out of greed performed that vile deed. / From intense greed, a great mire enters even into their hearts.
From that very mire, from fear and delusion, there was loss of understanding; / then, by the accumulation of sin, that city was burnt up.
The women were corrupt, the people were corrupt, all through the power of sin at that time. / An old dvija, an understander [of truth] there, did not set his mind on that practice.
His wife, a virtuous woman filled with great sorrow, / distressed by hardship, spoke to her husband about the practice of the city:

The brāhmaṇa woman said:
"Great distress is mine, O lord, seeing you afflicted with sorrow. / You ought to follow this practice of the village, or else some other."

Then he, knowing fault, smiled and spoke these words:
"He who lives by sin, having abandoned dharma, the supreme good,
he is a fool, O fortunate lady; he goes where there is no rebirth [in a good state]. / These dvijas of evil conduct, along with their wives and possessions,
through the practice of extreme sin, considered heinous sinners, / together with their immense sin, will go down to the underworld.
Having obtained non-rebirth in the end, there is no end to their transgression. / I alone remain here because of preserving my own merit."
Then she said to him: "Your words are laughable to people! / You should say this before us, not before anyone else."

The dvija said:
"If I go elsewhere from here, at that very moment, my dear, / the city, along with its wealth and own people, will go to the downward course."
Having said this, exceedingly pleased and taking his own wealth, / the twice-born went quickly with her to another border.
Having halted, he looked: the city stood firm just as before. / And the virtuous wife said to her husband: "This city is not destroyed."
The best of vipras, greatly astonished, said: "Let it be examined! / Has any property remained there outside our house?"
Reflecting, the virtuous woman said to her husband: "By mistake, a pair of shoes / was not brought by me; they remain there. What shall I wear?"
Having spoken thus to her husband, the virtuous woman fetched them and returned. / Close by her husband, the city was seen to have undergone effortless destruction.
Then the castes—vipras and others, the base inhabitants of the city— / remain in terrible hell, suffering, never to be reborn [well].
With hardship they go to the city of Yama, and there is no atonement for them. / Therefore that foul-smelling [food] is declared impure and to be avoided.
One who takes pleasure in eating as before, and even now commits sin, / inclined to theft, roaming by night—he should be known by the wise as a rogue.
Unwise in all undertakings, unacknowledged in all rites, / lacking conventional conduct, he is merely a foolish beast.
Thus there are camels and the like, mongooses and others that are edible; / hurtful, a source of anxiety to kinsmen, and a coward except in battle,
always fond of leftovers and the like—such a man is proclaimed by the wise to be a dog. / One who is constantly devoted to thievery, deceiving many friends,
ever quarrelling with his mate—such a mortal is proclaimed [to be like an animal]. / One who is by nature always fickle, ever unsteady about food,
a leaper fond of the woods—such a man on earth is an ape. / An informer by speech and thought among his own people and strangers,
because of being a producer of anxiety, such a man is deemed a snake. / Powerful, aggressive in character, and always shameless,
fond of rotting meat, an enjoyer—such a man is called a lion among men. / From his roar alone, others such as wolves cower in fear.
Those who are known among men as elephants and the like are far-seeing; / in this very manner, beginning with these, one should discern [them] among men.
We declare the characteristic of the gods established in human form: / devoted to the worship and austerities [in honour] of the twice-born, the gods, guests, / gurus, virtuous people, and ascetics;
always [devoted] to the treatises on dharma and the sciences of statecraft; / forgiving in nature, conquering anger, speaking the truth, self-restrained;
compassionate, beloved in the world, handsome, sweet-voiced; / a master of speech in all affairs, virtuous, capable, of great strength;
literate and learned, knowing the reality of song, dance, and poetry; / knowledgeable in all systems regarding the science of the self and other subjects, and in musical notes;
taking pleasure in all sacrificial food, in products of the cow, in vegetarian food, / in items of fresh taste, newly gathered, and very pleasing;
in perfumes, garlands, garments, sacred sciences, and ornaments; / delighted with guests, giving, and ceremonies such as the conjunction rites;
whose time passes with duties such as bathing and giving, with vows, sacrifices, / worship of the gods, and recitations; and whose day is never barren.
Such conduct of men is constantly [regarded as] virtuous; / conduct of men like that of gods is extolled by the best of sages.
Yet a god has an abundance of sattva, while a man is indeed fearful; / a god is always profound, whereas a man is ever soft.
Delight arises from the praise of the two, but never from a Daitya or the like, indeed. / An affectionate disposition is supreme happiness, friendship, merit, and good fortune.
Affection exists between divine and human [beings], and likewise between Daityas and Rākṣasas; / among spirits and the like towards spirits, and affection of a beast even for a beast.
Crows and others are fond of their own kind, and so are others towards their own kinds; / they are fond, and they are averse; know that this is their characteristic.
Thus, according to the distinction of merit among the particular kinds [of beings], / one should recognize the pleasing and the displeasing, merit and demerit, virtue and fault.
There is no happiness at all on earth for a married couple due to difference in kind among men; / affection exists among those of one's own kind, whether liberated or in hell.
From great merit do performers of virtuous deeds obtain a [good] life; / evil-minded men, who are Daityas and the like, meet an end [of suffering].
In the Kṛta age, gods were born on earth, not Daityas or other classes; / [one quarter were born] in the Tretā age, and two quarters in the Dvāpara age;
and in the twilight of the Kali age, all quarters are mixed together. / The emergence of gods and others came to be what brought about the Bhārata [war].
Those who were warriors of Duryodhana, and his armies and the like, / all those on earth, who were Karṇa and the rest, were Daityas and others.
Bhīṣma the son of Gaṅgā was the chief of the Vasus, and Drona was a lordly divine sage; / Aśvatthāman was Hara in person, and Hari was born in Nanda's line.
The Pāṇḍavas were born as five Indras, Vidura was Dharma himself, / and Gāndhārī, Draupadī, and Kuntī were goddesses on the surface of the earth.
In the midst of Kali, there are gods and Daityas; in the remainder, men are Daityas. / Pretas, flesh-eaters, beasts, and birds are continually born.
And their unchaste maidservant, ever distressed and younger, / always out of affection during their disputes, reported their conduct.
Those Daityas and others who are devoted to all sins, / to strife, and to unjust acts, are all destined for hell.

Vaiśaṃpāyana said: / Since the state of Daityas and the like is false, they have no divinity nor a place among gods. / How [can they have] enjoyment? How happiness, health, and accumulation of strength?
How can there be kingdom, lifespan, renown, what is desired and cherished, strength, / statecraft, knowledge, and so on, an eternal state developed from birth?
How can there be acts such as giving and study, sacrifices, and so on, O lord? / You ought to tell this to me, a trusted pupil, O venerable one.
Vyāsa said: / Certainly, the austerity of the Daityas arises entirely from rashness, / as do vows, sacrifices, and the like, and affection for one's own people.
One who is self-controlled, freed from defects, conversant with the meaning of the treatises on statecraft, / and purified by these diverse means, would have the characteristics of a god.
The twice-born who himself performs the virtuous rites / of the Purāṇas and Āgamas in heaven and here on earth is capable of sustaining the earth.
The one who, especially upon seeing a Vaiṣṇava, rejoices and worships [him], / is released from all sins; he is capable of sustaining the earth.
The brāhmaṇa devoted to the six duties, always engaged in all sacrifices, / ever fond of stories of dharma, is capable of sustaining the earth.
Those who betray trust, the ungrateful, the breakers of vows, / and those who hate the twice-born and the gods—such men tear down the earth.
Those who are wicked and addicted to liquor, likewise addicted to gambling, / and who converse with heretics and fallen men—such men tear down the earth.
Those who are devoid of good deeds, always perturbed and unrestrained, / agitated by the meaning of the treatises on Smṛti—such men tear down the earth.
Those who, abandoning their own occupation, practice a degraded one, / and who are devoted to reviling the guru out of hatred—such men tear down the earth.
Those who restrain a giver, who incite [others] to sin, / and who torment the poor and helpless—such men tear down the earth.
These and many other men who perform sinful deeds, / having caused persons to fall, tear down the earth.
He who hears this delightful, supreme secret of secrets, most beneficial, / suffers no misfortune, sorrow, bad luck, or poverty on earth.
He is not born among Daityas and the like; eternal happiness in heaven is his; / there is no untimely death for him, nor is he tainted by sins.
Here [on earth] he is the ruler over all people, and in heaven the lord of heaven; / having enjoyed heaven age after age, he sets forth on the path to liberation.

1.77.m: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: / This [being] continually rises in the sky, O best of the twice-born, O lord. / Who is this, or what is his splendour? Where was the lord of rays born?
What task indeed does he perform, because of which he is full of rays, / [and is] constantly to be worshipped by gods, best of sages, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Daityas, Rākṣasas,
all men, and the brāhmaṇas and others? / Vyāsa said: The supreme splendour of Brahmā issued forth from Brahmā's body.
Know it to be the very embodiment of Brahman, granting dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation; / a mass [of light] with pure rays, extremely fierce and most unbearable.
Seeing it, tormented by the fierce rays, the worlds fled in fear; / and thereupon all the oceans, the noble rivers, and streams,
the creatures there began to dry up, and distressed people were dying. / Then the gods, led by Śakra, approached Brahmā.
They spoke of this matter, and Brahmā said to the gods: / 'O gods, the primary origin of Brahmā's body is the lord who generates sattva;
this one, directly full of rajas, is the moon situated in the midst of the body. / By these two are the worlds, moving and unmoving, sustained in the triple world:
the gods who arise spontaneously, or those here born of a womb, / those born from eggs, those born from sweat, or those here born of plants and the like.
Indeed, we are not able to describe the majesty of this sun; / protected, brought forth, and sustained by him are the worlds, indeed.
There is none equal to him, on account of his guarding of all; / and by seeing him at daybreak, the mass of sin dissolves.
Having worshipped him, the twice-born attain liberation; / at the time of the twilight worship, indeed, the brāhmaṇas who know Brahman
stand with uplifted arms, and they are honoured by the gods. / And the goddess who is in his orb, whose nature is the twilight,
All dvijas, having worshipped [the Sun], attain heaven and liberation. / Those fallen on earth who are defiled are purified by his rays.
By mere worship at twilight, one becomes purified from sin. / Having seen a cāṇḍāla, a cow-killer, an outcaste, one afflicted with leprosy,
one contaminated by heinous sins or surrounded by secondary sins— / those men who look at the Sun are purified from grave sin.
By mere worship of him, one is freed from all disease; / neither blindness, nor poverty, nor sorrow, nor lamentation
does he obtain here or in the hereafter, having worshipped the Sun. / The gods such as Hari and Hara are never visible to the worlds;

they are accessible through meditation, but this deity is traditionally considered visible.
The gods said:
"May there be grace; may he be worshipped; and may there be veneration and homage!
Yet the very sight of him, O Brahman, is like the fire of cosmic dissolution. / All creatures, men and others on earth, have reached the state of death.
By the power of his radiance, the oceans and other waters have vanished. / We are not capable of enduring it; how then could ordinary people?
Therefore, through your grace, let a means be devised / so that we may worship the Sun, and men may sacrifice with devotion."
Having heard the words of the gods, Brahmā went to the lord of the skies. / Having gone, he began to praise him for the welfare of all the worlds:
"O god, you are the eye of the entire world, free from ailment, / assuming the form of Brahman in visible form, difficult to behold, the fire of cosmic dissolution!
For you reside within all the gods, always the friend of wind in the body; / the digestion of food and the like comes from you, and life certainly exists [through you].
Creation and dissolution, O god—you alone are the lord of the world. / Without you, there is not a single day's life for all the worlds.
You are the lord of all the worlds, the protector, guardian, father, and mother / of all moving and unmoving beings; by your grace the world is sustained.
Among all the gods, O Lord, there is none equal to you; / your real presence is everywhere; by you alone is the world upheld.
You cause form, fragrance, and the like; the sweetness of tastes is due to you. / Thus the Sun is the lord of the universe, the cause of the preservation of all.
Of holy places, sacred fields, sacrifices, and the world, O Lord, / you are the sole, attentive cause, the witness of all, a mine of virtues,
omniscient, the maker, destroyer, and protector of all, ever zealous, / destroying the mire of darkness and disease, destroying poverty and suffering,
the supreme relative in the hereafter and here, all-knowing, all-seeing. / Except for you, there is no benefactor of all the worlds."

The Sun said:
"O Forefather, great in wisdom, sovereign of the universe, creator of the universe! / Speak quickly what is supreme for you; I shall carry out your intention, O Ordainer."

Brahmā said:
"Your ray is exceedingly fierce and completely unbearable to the worlds. / Act in such a way, O lord of the gods, that it becomes mild."

The Sun said:
"My rays, tens of millions in number, are extremely destructive to the world / and do not bring about what is desired in the world. O Lord, cut them by your technique!"

Then, surely prompted by the Sun's words, Viriñci quickly
summoned Viśvakarman and fashioned a wheel made of thunderbolt,

and cut down the Sun's rays, which were like the fire of universal destruction.
Out of those very [rays], Viśvakarman then fashioned Viṣṇu's Sudarśana discus,

Yama's unerring staff, and likewise the trident of Paśupati;
and Kāla's supreme sword, and the spear delighting the master [Kārttikeya],

and the supreme weapon of Caṇḍikā, along with a wondrous pike.
By Brahmā's command, [all these] were quickly made by that very Viśvakarman.

A thousand rays were left, and the rest were pared away.
By the manner of a birthless manifestation, O sage, [he was born] once again from Kaśyapa,

born from the womb of Aditi, and so is known as Āditya.
He moves at the edge of the universe and also circles around the peak of Mount Meru,

always a hundred thousand yojanas above the earth, day and night.
The planets, headed by the moon, move there as ordained by the Creator.

The sun, consisting of twelve [forms], travels through the twelve months.
Because of his transition, his saṃkrānti is recognized by all.

Whatever fruit [accrues] to the worlds during them, we shall proclaim in full, O sage:
In Sagittarius, Gemini, Pisces, and Virgo are the Ṣaḍaśīti [transitions];

in Taurus, Scorpio, Aquarius, and Leo, [the transition] is known as Viṣṇupadī.
Know that the libation [given then] is imperishable, as are gifts and worship of the gods.

Eighty-six thousandfold is the fruit on a Ṣaḍaśīti;
on a Viṣṇupadī it is a hundred thousandfold, but on a solstice, it is myriad upon myriad.

Whatever gift is given during a Viṣṇupadī is declared to be imperishable.
I declare that the giver attains [divine] presence always, in birth after birth.

In the cold season, from giving a cotton quilt, no suffering arises in the body.
In giving gold equal to one's weight or in giving a bed, the fruit of both is imperishable.

One who, free from jealousy, gives a bed furnished with all accessories
to an eminent brahmin among the castes, obtains the rank of king.

Likewise, having given fire and water on a riverbank or on the road in the early morning,
and having given oil and betel leaf, one becomes the lord of the earth.

Having bowed to the twice-born with sincerity and truthfulness, a wealthy man attains imperishability.
In the month of Māgha, in the dark fortnight, on the fifteenth day at the break of dawn,

having gratified the ancestors with water and sesame seeds, one becomes imperishable in heaven.
And having given an auspicious cow with golden horns and the luster of jewels,

with silver hooves and a fine bronze milking pail—
having given this to an eminent brahmin, one becomes a universal king;

having given food and ornaments, a king becomes a sovereign ruler and lord of wealth.
Moreover, one who gives a cow made of sesame, equipped with all implements,

is freed from sins accumulated over seven lifetimes and becomes imperishable in heaven.
Having given wholesome cooked food to a brahmin, one enjoys imperishable heaven.

Whatever grain, clothing, servant, house, seat, and the like
one gives to an eminent brahmin, fortune never abandons that person.

Whatever gift is given, whether small or great,
is imperishable in other worlds, and likewise on the days of the beginning of the cosmic ages.

Or worship of the gods, praise, listening to recitations of dharma—
[all this] purifies from all sins, and that person becomes worthy of worship in heaven.

The third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha is remembered as a Manvantarā.
Whatever gift is given on it is said to be completely imperishable:

wealth, enjoyment, and likewise kingship, and heaven lasting through another cosmic age.
Therefore, giving and honoring the virtuous yield infinite fruit after death.

The Manvantarā in Māgha, however, is the seventh lunar day of the bright [fortnight];
it is declared the most meritorious lunar day, preserved by the Purāṇas.

The seventh lunar day in the bright fortnight of Māgha is equal to ten million suns;
fasting on that auspicious day, a person is liberated—there is no doubt about this.

For the bright seventh of Māgha is equal to a solar eclipse;
bathing at dawn on that day yields great fruit.

“And whatever sin has been committed by me across seven births,
may this seventh lunar day sacred to the Sun destroy that sickness and sorrow of mine!

Mother of all beings, O seventh day of the seven-horsed [Sun],
when the seventh day has dawned, O goddess, homage to you in the orb of the sun!”

Arka leaves, barley, flowers, fragrant substances, and jujube fruits,
brought together in that leaf or in a copper vessel with rice,

a sacrificial thread, and with vermilion, having offered a splendid guest-offering,
all sin committed across seven births goes to destruction.

Only so long is one tormented by hells, diseases, and sorrow-giving sins.
One should feed [a brahmin] sacrificial food, pure, made with sun-dried rice,

and one should avoid ginger ground on a stone, leafy vegetables,
leaves of the kodo millet, plantain, and goat's ghee.

Hairs, insects, and the like are to be avoided, as well as bathing in hot water;
one should avoid all tiny seeds and the like during the vow to the Sun.

And the vow-keeper should not perform any other deed there without contemplation on dharma;
the solar vow is of great merit, praised by the Purāṇas.

For thousands of crores and hundreds of crores of years,
one obtains eternal enjoyment in heaven equal to that of the Sun.

Even upon the exhaustion of heaven in this way, one is born as a king on earth, very wealthy;
in the mortal realm, from past practice, he performs the vow of the Sun.

Thus he personally obtains happiness and eternal enjoyment in heaven;
through the grace of the Sun, the embodied soul attains health and prosperity.

And the seventh lunar day of the bright fortnight of Māgha falling on a Sunday
is renowned as Mahājayā; elsewhere it is known as Vijayā.

Vijayā yields a myriad hundred-thousandfold, while Mahājayā yields infinite [fruit];
there, by that one vow alone, one is liberated from the bondage of rebirth.

One who gives an excellent horse, gold, red cloth, and grain
out of devotion to the Sun becomes successively lord of heaven and earth.

I shall explain their distinction; listen faithfully, O brahmin!
One who gives an excellent mount adorned with fine ornaments here,

reaches an earth surrounded by the seven oceans and rid of enemies;
in another human life, he becomes sole ruler by means of that one [gift].

Or a vehicle without horses, adorned even with bulls—
a māṣa or two māṣas of gold is ordained by the wise as the sacrificial fee.

A vessel of gems of great value, or whatever is fashioned of gold—
having given gold alone, one becomes a lord of wealth in heaven.

One who gives red cloth and grain according to one's capacity
attains sovereignty over heaven and earth; fortune never abandons him.

Free of disease, of serene mind, conqueror of robbers, glorious,
as long as the sun shines, he is most highly revered.

At the beginning of Māgha, one should perform the twelfth and the mystical seventh;
having enjoyed one's desired reward in this world, one is revered by the gods.

A wise man, having duly performed the Arkāṅgasaptamī vow,
purified from sin, obtains his desire in this world and attains liberation;
And I will declare the characteristic and the rite month by month, / and by the grace of this vow, one is worshipped among the gods in heaven.

In the bright fortnight, on a Sunday, when the sun's northern course has commenced,
under a masculine asterism, one should undertake the Saptamī vow.

Hasta, Anurādhā, and Puṣya, Śravaṇa, Mṛgaśīrṣa, and Punarvasu—
these the wise declare to be masculine asterisms.

A single meal on the fifth [tithi], a night meal on the sixth is prescribed,
fasting on the seventh, and on the eighth the breaking of the fast should occur.

The tip of an arka plant, pure cow dung, good black pepper, water, and fruit he consumes, / a root, and fasting at night, having properly performed eating only a single meal likewise.

Milk or food smeared with clarified butter—these are prescribed in this order; / having observed the seventh day of the Sun, one attains the desired fruit.

The tip of an arka plant: two distinct small leaves situated at the end of a branch of an arka shrub located to the north-east of the village should be drunk with water, untouched by teeth.

Pure cow dung not fallen on the ground, taken with middle finger and thumb to the measure of a pala, should be drunk with water, untouched by teeth; / good black pepper, unblemished, not stale, large, not dried up, one [grain], should be drunk with water, untouched by teeth.

Water flowing from the root of the fingers sacred to Brahmā and the ancestors should be drunk; / fruit: one among dates or coconuts should be drunk, untouched by teeth.
Food smeared with clarified butter should be the size of a peacock’s egg, / and the clarified butter too should be of that same measure.
When the sun makes a person's shadow twice their height, / one should know that to be the nakta; the nakta is not eating at night.
First one should worship the deity with mantras and with fruits, flowers, and the like; / then one should perform the gift of food in the measure stated by the rule.
Then the meditation: endowed with all auspicious marks, adorned with all ornaments, / two-armed, red-colored, and holding red lotuses in his hands,
an orb of brilliance situated in the midst of abundant water, with his retinue, / seated upon a lotus-throne, the god anointed with red fragrant paste—
one should contemplate the god Āditya, especially at the time of worship. / Now this is the mantra: 'We know the Sun; we meditate on the thousand-rayed one; may the Sun inspire us.'
This supreme recitation is declared to bring victory on the seventh day, / [offering] karavīra and karañja blossoms resembling red saffron.
Afterward, the breaking of the fast is to be performed, especially on the eighth day; / it must be done on the eighth day itself, never breaking the fast on the ninth.
One does not attain the fruit of the vow if the fast is broken on the ninth day. / The breaking of the fast, however, [should be done] in the afternoon, avoiding pungent, bitter, and sour foods.
One should carefully clean the rice, removing grass seeds and the like; / one should avoid mung beans, black gram, sesame seeds, and ghee.
If capable, one should feed brāhmaṇas with devotion, using oblations such as milk, / or according to one’s ability with food, drinks, and meatless condiments.
One should give a fee to the brāhmaṇa, distributing it appropriately. / The person who observes this seventh-day vow that bestows endless fruit,
which pacifies all sins and increases wealth and sons— / having observed the vow month after month to please the Sun, O best of the twice-born,
whoever breaks the fast with devotion goes to the realm of the Sun. / He dwells in heaven for ten million kalpas and then reaches the supreme state.
This very supreme secret was spoken of old by Śambhu; / from constantly hearing it, from keeping this vow, / or from reciting it to people, equal fruit is proclaimed.

1.78.m: Vaiśampāyana said: / O venerable one, by your grace I have heard the purifying vow; / I wish to hear another that is dear to the Sun.
Vyāsa said: / Having bowed his head to the ground before Maheśvara, who was seated comfortably on the delightful peak of Kailāsa, Skanda spoke these words:
"The rite named Arkāṅga has been heard from you in detail by me in this way; / O lord, I wish to hear truly the fruit of [observing] the days of the week and the like."
The Lord said: / A man observing the vow should offer water-oblation with red flowers on Sunday; / eating at the nakta hour the food of sacrificial oblation, he does not fall from heaven.
And the Supreme Lord together with his retinue feels delight / for one who performs the entire virtuous conduct of the seventh day on the day of the Sun.
By observing the day of the week and the lunar day, one becomes equal to a hero; / by that one [act], he attains leadership of the attendants for as long as the Sun is in the sky.
Bestowing all desires, meritorious, granting sovereignty, destroying disease, / granting heaven, granting liberation, and meritorious—the vow on Sunday is beneficial.
On Sunday, on a solar transit, and on the seventh day, O Śivā, / vow, worship, and water-offering on that day all become imperishable.
On a bright Sunday, the thorough worship of the lord of the planets [is performed]; / drawing it forth from the mouth through the fire of the life-breath, one should install it in the diagram.

Having meditated on him as having two arms, seated on a red lotus, with a beautiful neck, wearing red garments, and adorned with all red ornaments, one should take a flower in both hands, smell it, and throw it in the north-east.
"We know the Āditya; we meditate on the light-maker; / may that Bhānu inspire us."
Then [there is] the anointing according to the rule taught by the teacher; / at the end of the anointing, good incense, and at the end of the incense, a lamp;
at the end of the lamp, an offering of food, and then one should offer water; / then one should perform recitation, praise, the hand gestures, and obeisance.
The añjali is known as the first gesture, and the second is the dhenukā. / One who worships Arka in this manner attains communion with Ravi.
My dreadful [sin of] killing a Brahmin, the skull clinging to my hand, / was released on the bank of Vārāṇasī by the grace of that Ravi.
There is no deity in the three worlds higher than Ravi, / by whose grace I was released from the terrible, heavy sin.
Skanda said: / Having heard your word, O Lord, wonder arose in me, O master: / there is no god other than you; how could there be the killing of a Brahmin in you?
You are the Lord of knowledge, a yogin, the experiencer in the worlds, imperishable, immutable; / you are the sole teacher of the gods, the all-pervading Maheśvara,
all-knowing, ever the giver of boons, the sovereign of all living beings. / Whence could you have misdeeds, O Lord, or especially anger?
Śiva said: / For the benefit of the worlds, having become distinct in each cosmic age, / we do everything, O son—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
We have neither bondage nor liberation, nor what is not to be done, nor what is to be done; / nevertheless, for the protection of the world, we act according to rule.
[He is] the supreme whole, the destroyer of all obstacles, / the alleviator of all diseases, the accomplisher of all aims.
The blameless one, having become manifold though single due to the division of time, / blazes month after month; the single one attains a twelvefold nature.
[He is] Mitra in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa; in Pauṣa, eternal Viṣṇu; / Varuṇa in the month of Māgha; and Sūrya in Phālguna.
Bhānu blazes in the month of Caitra; in Vaiśākha he is known as Tāpana; / Indra blazes in the month of Jyeṣṭha; in Āṣāḍha blazes Ravi.
Gabhasti [blazes] in the month of Śrāvaṇa; Yama in Bhādrapada; / Hiraṇyaretas in Āśvayuja; and Divākara in Kārtika.
Thus these twelve Ādityas have been proclaimed month by month, / of vast form, of great brilliance, possessing the radiance of the fire of cosmic dissolution.
Whoever recites this daily has no sin; / no disease, no poverty, and no dishonor will befall him anywhere.
He obtains inexhaustible heaven, happiness, sovereignty, and fame in turn. / I shall declare the great mantra, supreme and productive of all delight:
"Oṃ, obeisance to the thousand-armed one, obeisance, obeisance to the Āditya! / Obeisance to you who hold a lotus in hand, obeisance, obeisance to Varuṇa!
Obeisance to the destroyer of darkness, obeisance, obeisance to holy Sūrya! / Obeisance to the thousand-tongued one, and obeisance, obeisance to Bhānu!
You are Brahmā, you are Viṣṇu, and you are Rudra; obeisance, obeisance! / You are fire among all beings, and you are wind; obeisance, obeisance!
Omnipresent among all beings, indeed nothing exists without you; / you abide in all bodies in this moving and unmoving universe."
Having recited thus, one obtains desire, heavenly enjoyment, and the like in order: / 'Āditya, Bhāskara, Sūrya, Arka, Bhānu, Divākara.'
Suvarṇaretas, Mitra, Pūṣan, and Tvaṣṭṛ are the ten; / Svayambhū and Timiranāśa are proclaimed as the eleventh and twelfth.
The pure person who recites these names of Sūrya / is freed from all sin and disease, and goes to the supreme state.
Again I shall declare another [set of names] of the great-souled Bhāskara, / which are named 'red', resembling red, with bodies red like vermilion.
Listen to those principal names, O six-faced one: / Tapana, Tāpana, the maker, the destroyer, the lord of the planets,
the witness of the world in the three worlds, the lord of the sky, Divākara, / having fire in his womb, the great priest, heaven, having seven horses as his mount,
lotus in hand, the piercer of darkness, the Ṛgveda, the Yajus, the singer of the Sāman, / dear to time, the lotus, and contemplated as the primal abode.
Whoever remembers these always with devotion—whence could he have fear of disease? / Listen carefully, O Kārttikeya, to the auspicious [mantra] which destroys all sin;
not the slightest doubt should be entertained regarding the Āditya, O wise one: / "Oṃ, obeisance to Indra; Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu."
This is the recitation, the fire sacrifice, and the twilight worship; / it brings all peace and destroys all obstacles.
It destroys all diseases: spider-bite poison, boils, and so forth, / jaundice and other sicknesses, and whatever diseases are dreadful;
tertian, quotidian, and quartan fevers, / leprosy, consumption, abdominal disease, and fever;
gravel, strangury, and various ailments and afflictions, / diseases born of wind, and diseases born of the womb.
The great tormenting diseases, afflictive and painful, / all go to dissolution by the mere utterance of [the name of] Āditya.
"Protect me, O god of gods, in dangers from planets and diseases!" / All of them are calmed when Divākara is praised.
I shall declare the root mantra of the great-souled Bhāskara, / which fulfills all desires and aims, and ever grants enjoyment and liberation.
And this is the mantra: "hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ sūryāya namaḥ". / By this mantra, all success will surely come about constantly.
Diseases will not afflict him, nor will there be misfortune or fear. / But whoever takes water energized by the sun, in proper order,
by the mere drinking of it, a man is freed from disease. / It should not be given, it should not be proclaimed, but it should be recited with diligence.
To those who are not devotees, to the childless, and to heretics and worldly people [it should not be given]; / mixed with mustard oil, one should administer it in nasal drops and in a drink.
[By] water energized by the sun, O son, one is freed from all disease. / The root mantra should be recited at twilight and in sacrificial rites;
when it is recited, diseases and cruel planets are destroyed. / What need is there of many other treatises or extensive mantras?
This is all-pacifying, O child, and accomplishes all aims. / It should not be given to an atheist, nor to a reviler of the gods and Brahmins.
It should be given to one devoted to the teacher, and never to others. / The mortal who, having risen in the morning, will recite it daily,
even if a killer of a cow or ungrateful, is freed from all sins; / and it produces bodily health, increases wealth, and brings fame.
There is no doubt that Divākara is pleased with him. / Whether once, twice, or thrice a day, constantly,
he who recites it in the presence of Ravi obtains the desired fruit: / one desiring a son obtains a son; one desiring a maiden obtains a maiden;
one desiring knowledge obtains knowledge; one desiring wealth obtains wealth. / One who listens endowed with devotion and accompanied by pure conduct,
freed from all sins, goes even to the world of Sūrya. / And whatever [is recited] during an observance of Bhāskara, in rituals of vows, and in sacrifices,
if recited in holy places and pilgrimage sites, it becomes multiplied ten million fold. / In feedings for the planets, in worship, in feeding Brahmins, or before the twice-born,
the Brahmin who recites this obtains infinite fruit. / The wise person before ascetics, Brahmins, and gods,
who recites it or causes it to be recited, is glorified in the world of the gods.

1.79.m: Vyāsa said: / In the middle country there was an independent sovereign known as Bhadreśvara, / purified by many austerities and by various kinds of vows.
He indeed always worshipped the gods with a noble disposition; / [yet] on his left hand there arose leprosy, which became white.
Then, because of the application of physicians, the sign had been seen beforehand; / summoning the foremost twice-born and his ministers, he spoke these words.
The king said: / "O brāhmaṇas, an unbearable sin has arisen on my hand, condemned by people; / therefore, [tell me of] a sacred great field where I may cast off my body.
Instruct me, O knowers of dharma, for the benefit of the next world; / for me, who am devoid of lineage, O valiant ones, [tell me] what is beneficial after death and in the hereafter.
Speak that to me graciously, so that I may do what is directed." / The twice-born said: / "If the kingdom is abandoned by you, who are wise and devoted to dharma,
this world will be ruined, O king; therefore you ought not to speak [thus]. / Indeed, this remedy for it is understood by us:
With mantras, diligently worship the Sun, the great god, O lord!" / The king said: / "By what means, O lords of brāhmaṇas, shall I satisfy the Sun?
Because of impure leprosy, which is despised by people, / I am unfit to be seen by all beings, and despised, O twice-born!
What shall I do with kingship, and what could come of worship?" / The twice-born said: / "Staying here in your own kingdom, and worshipping the Sun,
freed from terrible sin, you will attain heaven and liberation." / Having heard this, the king of kings, bowing low to the best of the twice-born,
performed that supreme worship of the Sun / with daily worship and mantras, offerings, and unguents,
with various fruits, water-oblations, and unbroken sun-dried grains of rice, / with hibiscus flowers, leaves of arka, karavīra, and karañja,
with red saffron, vermilion, and spring jasmine and the like, / with fragrant plantain leaves and their charming fruits.
Having prepared the arghya in a vessel of udumbara wood, the king, facing the Sun, / always gave it to the Sun, accompanied continually by his ministers and royal priests.
The arghya was offered on all sides by the chief queens and concubines, / by all the residents of the inner apartments, and by the guards together with their wives,
and by the servant classes and others, day after day, / with fierce rites of sun-propitiation, and with supreme hymns and mantras.
They worshipped the Maker of Day with the root-mantra and other mantras; / and likewise, with fully composed minds, they performed the other vow of Arkāṅga.
Gradually, after completing a year, the king reached the end of the disease; / when the terrible ailment was removed, that king caused the whole world
to be disciplined and made [them] perform the vow of worship at dawn: / likewise with hibiscus flowers, fragrant plantain fruit,
touching with arrows and wives, arka leaves and flowerless offerings— / thus having performed great merit, he became beloved by all people.
Living on sacrificial food, without [other] food, the people worshipped the Sun. / In this very manner the Sun was worshipped by them according to the three classes.
Well-pleased, he came to the king and spoke these words with compassion: / 'Choose a boon, whatever is cherished in your mind,
for the benefit of all of you, your followers, and the city dwellers.' / The king said: 'If you wish to grant a boon, O Eye of All, dear to me,
let there be the highest heaven in your presence for all of us.' / The Sun said: 'Your ministers, these twice-born brāhmaṇas, along with their wives and attendants,
endowed with youthful vigor and pure, until the dissolution of beings, / let them abide in my charming city, free from disease, with all enjoyments.
With heavenly trees in full bloom, with palaces resembling desire-granting trees, / with celestial women, O highly fortunate one, and with supreme dances, songs, and the like,
after five cosmic cycles, O king, you shall become a king at the beginning of a Manu's era. / These people of yours, O king, the city dwellers and the priests,
as well as the inhabitants of the countryside, the wise men and the wealthy people, / having received a boon from me there, you shall easily attain heaven.'
Having spoken thus, the Eye of the World vanished right there. / Then King Bhadreśvara rejoiced in heaven together with his city.
Even those who were insects and the like there, protected along with their offspring, / enjoy immense, wondrous pleasures in heaven at the divine trees.
In this very way, kings, brāhmaṇas, and sages of praiseworthy vows, / and those castes such as kṣatriyas, swiftly went to the heaven of the Sun.
By some, wealth was requested, and by others sons and wives, / [as well as] happiness, heaven, and health, by the grace of the Sun.
Whatever pure person reads this auspicious mass of merit, / his sins are all destroyed, and he is revered on earth like Rudra.
He shall become a witness of all in heaven, a granter of boons, dear to the Sun. / A self-controlled mortal who hears it shall obtain his desired fruit.
He goes beyond all sins; in the assembly of the Sun himself / he shall ever be eloquent; from listening [to this], he becomes meritorious and wealthy.
This secret of secrets was proclaimed by the Sun; / this was told to Yama and declared on earth by Vyāsa.

1.80.m: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: / 'By your grace, this power of the lord of planets has been heard. / Speak to us, O twice-born, of the propitiation of the planets beginning with the Sun.
Who are they, the planets beginning with the Sun? How is their satisfaction [achieved], and what pleases them? / When time and place arrive, what is their auspicious and inauspicious sight?'
Vyāsa said: / 'The planets and others in the world experience good and evil deeds; / indeed, they bring about the auspicious and the inauspicious to exhaust the karma of the universe.
The Sun should be known as Time and the End among men and among planets; / through his union with fierce and mild [influences], he is the lord in restraint and grace.
Because of his planetary nature, I shall state his satisfaction: / One who makes an oblation with the sprouts of the udumbara and the palāśa,
with the root-mantra "By the dark [path]" for the sake of pacification, / should offer [oblations] combined with clarified butter, for the sake of attaining the desired fruit.
For the pacification of all diseases, and for deliverance from slaughter and bondage, / one hundred offerings should be made with each mantra.
And one should offer a well-prepared goat to the Sun on a Sunday; / one should feed brāhmaṇas according to one's means with charming food for gods and ancestors.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight, and likewise on the fifteenth, / a diseased person is freed from disease and does not undergo distress from disease.
The supreme and immortal being, extending from Brahmā down to a clump of grass, / in the universe and in the atom, the Sun is revered [in all].

He causes all from beginning to end in due order, because he is the cause of origination and maintenance; / at the creation of life for beings, he is the protector wandering through the universe in the body.
At the time of death, he departs from within the body along with the vital breath. / The Moon, ever stationed at the top of the head, endowed with sixteen digits,
day and night rains down a shower of nectar in the body, facing downwards. / Living beings survive through it, whether great creatures or tiny as atoms.
On the earth he nourishes crops, and likewise motionless and moving beings. / By these two luminaries the world is sustained and brought forth.
From the worship of the two, nourishment is ever meritorious and boundless; / a practitioner who is always pure shall accomplish all objectives.
That lowest of men who out of delusion does not worship the Moon— / his lifespan comes to an end, and he goes to hell.
O bearer of spotless digits, crest-jewel of the bearer of the Gaṅgā! / On the second day [of the fortnight], O Lord of the World, O Moon, obeisance be to you!
And whatever man, upon reaching another lunar day, performs / salutation even to the Moon, he shall obtain the desired fruit.
O fortunate one born from the eye of Atri, born from the churning of the milk-ocean, / whose abode is on the crown of the Great Lord, O Moon, obeisance be to you!
O divine-formed one, obeisance to you, maker of nectar, lord of the world! / The wise know [this] in the bright fortnight as well as in the dark, in the night.

"Oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ, obeisance to Soma" is the mantra to be recited; / it is to be muttered at dawn. Whoever worships Soma thus, recites [this] or listens to it, / shall become like nectar in the world, birth after birth.
Whoever praises and worships him thus on earth with the thousand names, / attains imperishable heaven, from which return is hard to obtain.'
Thus the worship of Soma. In a brass vessel or in a bronze vessel full of curd and auspicious ghee, / whether less or more according to one's wealth, having heard of the rite free from envy,
or in gold, or in silver, on a Wednesday in the dark fortnight, / having installed Mercury in every station, one should give it to a man with many sons.
Supreme good fortune arises, far greater than nectar; / and there is never misfortune for women or for men.
'Desiring beauty and good fortune, I give this vessel filled with curds, / placed in a bronze bowl: grant me beauty and good fortune!'
A man free from envy should give this to a twice-born after uttering these words; / a sacrificial fee should be given according to one's means, as well as new garments and the like,
wholesome food with all accompaniments, delightful betel, / flower garlands and the like one should give for the sake of beauty and good fortune.
Whoever makes a gift in this manner to a twice-born, dedicated to Soma, / shall enjoy beauty and good fortune in heaven or in the world of mortals.

1.81.m: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: / 'The origin of the red-bodied one and his satisfaction among people, / his power, majesty, and splendor, I wish to hear in truth.'
Vyāsa said: / 'The deity born of a portion of Hara, born from the earth, the son of the Earth, / abiding in sattva, full of sattva, a hero wielding a spear on the earth,
a sharp, cruel planet, a radiant god with a red body, / a youth endowed with beauty, a powerful lord of lightning strikes.
By him daityas, flesh-eaters, and enemies of the gods were scorched, / as are human beings, sprouting plants, beasts, and birds by the influence of his planetary period.'
Vaiśaṃpāyana said: / 'How was this son of the Earth born from Śambhu? / How did he become a cruel planet and deity? This I wish to know.
How may his satisfaction arise for all worlds at all times? / O teacher, regarding me as devoted, speak without doubt from your mouth.'
Vyāsa said: / In the family of Hiraṇyākṣa was an intelligent king of the asuras, / renowned as Andhaka, a daitya who brought an end to all the gods.
He was born from a boon granted by Viṣṇu, and possessed the prowess of Viṣṇu. / By him alone were the gods, along with Indra and the enjoyers of sacrifices, vanquished one after another.
Then the gods went to Brahmā and spoke these words: / 'Our sovereignty, happiness, and sacrifices have been taken away by Andhaka alone.
Therefore let a means for his slaying be declared, and let it be carried out.' / Then the Creator addressed the gods: 'He has no death,
by virtue of Viṣṇu's boon and from the consuming of nectar. / However, so that his demoniac nature may surely be overcome,
for the welfare of the world, I shall produce desire joined with longing. / Doubt will surely enter there, yet he will pursue enjoyment with every woman.
Leaving aside Durgā, Pārvatī alone, his mind will not remain steadfast. / Then the enraged Lord of the World will reduce him to deformity.
Then, abandoning his demoniac nature, he will become his attendant (gaṇa).' / Having spoken thus, the Lord of Creatures sent desire joined with longing,
along with doubt and his own delusive power (māyā), against him. / Moved by passion, he then became intent on seeking out women.
Because of doubt, he looked neither upon his own wives nor upon other women. / Then, impelled by delusive power, he wandered through the three worlds.
On the ridge of the Himavat, he saw an exceedingly lovely gem among women. / Beholding Pārvatī, the daitya fell under the sway of desire.
Due to the loss of judgment, he desired to seize Durgā. / But Umā transformed her own body into the form of Koṭavī,
and stayed near Īśvara, while that lustful one sought to seize her. / Then, deprived of his senses by lust and with his mind driven mad,
the foremost daitya did not abandon Śiva, the sustainer, Pārvatī. / Then, emerging from meditation, Pārvatī's husband arrived.
Seeing him, the lord of daityas retreated to his own abode. / Having prepared his warriors, he was eager to conquer Śambhu,
bent on carrying off Gaurī alone, senseless from the delusion of desire. / Hearing this, the thirty gods, dispatched by Nandin, went against him
and fought a great battle, terrible and causing dread throughout the worlds. / The daityas who died in the battle were revived by the preceptor of the daityas.
All of them reported this news at Kailāsa. / Out of anger, Śambhu then addressed Nandin with these words:
'Go quickly to the abode of the daityas by my command, hero! / Before the eyes of all the daityas and in the assembly of the lord of the daityas,
seize that evil-minded descendant of Bhṛgu firmly by the hair, / and having seized him, bring him bewildered to my presence in an instant!'
Then the glorious Nandin, the lord of attendants, urged on by the husband of Pārvatī, / seized Kāvya by the hair by force in the presence of the daityas.
As he was bringing him away, the daityas struck him with weapons and arrows. / Yet they were unable to inflict any harm upon the powerful Nandin.
Holding him by the hair in front of the gods, / Nandin, delighted, came together with him before Hara.
Seizing the descendant of Bhṛgu, the preceptor of the asuras, with fury, / Śambhu, the lord of terrible form, equal to the end-making Yama, swallowed him.
Then the powerful lord of the daityas, enraged and surrounded by all his army, / rushed upon Śaṅkara there with dreadful weapons and missiles.
The thirty gods as well, and likewise the vidyādharas and others, enraged, / advanced into battle there against the daityas with great fury.
At that moment, a terrible, formidable battle arose / between the gods and the dānavas, striking terror into all the worlds.
Then, with trusty weapons, the gods struck down the dānavas, / and the sons of Danu struck down the immortals there in that great battle.
With arrows fashioned of gold, like thunderbolts, / and feathered with jewels, they pierced one another, each seeking victory.
With radiant [arrows] they brightly illuminated their bodies and the skies. / Slain by multitudes of unfailing weapons, the mighty daityas
were brought down by the foremost of the gods, the descendants of Kaśyapa. / The vast army that pervaded the world, well-equipped with weapons and forces,
was brought to destruction in an instant by all the gods with their trusty weapons, / and through the effort of Mahādeva himself who was fighting.
Though held aloft on the trident for a long time without being destroyed, Andhaka, with a humbled mind, / was made into an attendant (gaṇa), named Bhṛṅgīriṭi, O twice-born.
Then, having addressed the gods, Śiva vomited forth Śukra. / A fetus fell upon the earth, and therefore he is remembered as Bhauma.
Having addressed Śiva, Śukra went joyfully to the daityas. / Thus was born Bhauma, a portion of Hara, sprung from the earth.

His worship is to be performed by those of good vows on the fourth lunar day, on a Tuesday, / and when there is an astrological evil in a planetary period (daśā) or when he enters an unfavorable sign in transit (gocara),
in a triangular diagram (maṇḍala) with red flowers and ointments. / Worshiped thus indeed, Bhauma grants intellect, wealth,
sons, happiness, and fame. What more do you wish to hear?' / Vyāsa said: 'This auspicious narrative of righteousness has been told to you, O disciples,
hearing which one is never born again nor dies, / which bestows merit upon the twice-born and is to be attended upon by those desiring good fortune.
Go happily at your pleasure, having accomplished your purpose by my command.' / Brahmā said: Having recited this, the venerable Vyāsa, son of Satyavatī,
having determined varied righteousness, went to Śamyāprāsa, O son. / You too, my child, having understood the truth with faith, at your pleasure
wander at will, joyfully singing praise to Hari, / instructing people in righteousness and pleasing the preceptor of the worlds.
Pulastya said: / Addressed thus, O king, Nārada went to the Gandhamādana mountain / to see Nārāyaṇa, the best of sages, in the hermitage of Badarī.

1.82.m: Bhīṣma said: / The worship of Sūrya, Candra, and Bhauma has been heard. / Now relate the worship of Budha, the son of Soma.
Pulastya said: / Budha, born from the womb of Tārā, is the youthful son of Candra; / he should be known as a mild or cruel planet, bestowing auspicious and inauspicious results upon men.
The diagram (maṇḍala) for Budha is renowned to have the shape of an arrow. / One should make the diagram with powders of a color equal to emeralds.
One should worship him there with perfumes and the like, with lovely flowers and incenses, / and should make gifts according to rule when there is adversity in a planetary period or transit,
giving camphor, kidney beans, a green cloth, an emerald, / and gold according to one's capacity, for the satisfaction of Bodhana.
[Saying:] 'O son of Soma, of great wisdom, master of the Vedas and auxiliary sciences! / Salutations to you, stationed in the midst of the planets; be ever gracious to me.'
having thus praised Budha with devotion and a concentrated mind, O great king, / one would attain all desires by the grace of the son of Soma.
The worship of Guru is declared to be in a diagram shaped like a sword, / formed, O king, with beautiful yellow-colored powders.
One should worship him with yellow, fragrant flowers, with garments, and with gold, / and make gifts according to one's capacity when there is malefic influence in a planetary period or transit.
Split chickpeas, yellow cloth, gold, / and a topaz one should give to a Brahmin to pacify misfortune:
“O Bṛhaspati, teacher of the gods, skilled in all scriptures! / Pleased with this gift, be gentle towards me now!”
When this is done, O king of kings, the Guru becomes favorable; / a man attains all desires through the proper worship of Guru.
I shall also declare the worship of Bhārgava now, O king, / by performing which all desires are thoroughly fulfilled for men.
