A five-cornered diagram is prescribed for Bhārgava, / made with white powders according to rule by a wise man.
With white fragrances and flowers, and likewise with white garments, / a man endowed with faith should worship Bhārgava with devotion.
The gift of silver as a sacrificial fee is proclaimed according to one's capacity; / and when misfortune arises in a planetary period or transit, one should give a white horse.
Rice grains, white cloth, silver, and sandalwood, / and fragrant camphor should be given as a gift to a twice-born.
“O son of Bhṛgu, most fortunate one, family priest of the Dānavas! / Pleased with this gift, be benevolent, O you who are worshiped by all Asuras!”
Having uttered this mantra, he should make a gift as prescribed; / Bhārgava becomes pleased with him at once, O joy of the Kurus.
For the worship of Śanaiścara, having made a human-shaped diagram / with black powders, one should worship there with devotion.
With black fragrances, flowers, and likewise with garments of that kind, / iron as a sacrificial fee, and sesame oil-cake,
a gift in the misfortune caused by Śanaiścara: a black cow, black cloth, / and gold according to one's capacity, and likewise a sapphire one should give:
“O son of Sūrya, most fortunate one, son of Chāyā, of mighty power! / O downward-looking Śani, be gracious because of this gift!”
Having praised Śani with devotion in this way, he who gives to a twice-born, / to him Śani becomes favorable, even when malefic in transit.
The color and other particulars of Rāhu are all like those of Śani; likewise the diagram / is prescribed in the shape of the sun; the worship there is like that of the son of Arka.
Hessonite, mustard seeds, sesame seeds, and black gram, / a she-buffalo, and likewise a goat are declared to be the gift for Rāhu:
“O son of Siṃhikā, lord of the Daityas, Rāhu, crusher of the moon and sun! / O most fortunate one of good vows, be pleased with this gift!”
For Ketu, one should make a very splendid banner-shaped diagram; / the worship, color, and everything else should be known to be like that of Śani, O king.
The seven grains along with gold are prescribed as the gift for Ketu; / when this is done, they both become favorable to men, O king.
They bestow wealth, sons, happiness, and good fortune. / “Ā kṛṣṇena” is the mantra of Ravi, and “Imaṃ devāḥ” likewise of the moon.
“Agnir mūrdhā” is the mantra of Bhauma to be chanted in worship; / “Udbudhyadhvam” is of the son of Indu; of Guru Bṛhaspati likewise,
“Annāt pari” is of Śukra; this “Śaṃ no devīḥ” is of Śani; / and “Kayā naḥ” is of Rāhu; for Ketu, “Ketuṃ kṛṇvan” is remembered.
These mantras are prescribed in the worship and chanting for the planets. / When this is done, O best of kings, all planets become favorable
constantly to men, and they bestow abundant prosperity. / All this has been declared by me to you here in order, O great king.
Having heard this essence of the meaning of all scripture, a man goes to the presence of Īśvara. / This is purifying, an abode of renown; this is exceedingly dear to the ancestors.

And this serves as nectar among the gods, and brings merit to sinful men. / He who recites this renown-giving text, who hears it here with devotion, or witnesses worship to the enemy of Madhu and Mura,
and gives understanding to people, is worshiped in the world of Indra for one kalpa by Brahmā, Śiva, and the chiefs of the gods. / He who constantly listens to this auspicious deeds of the sages,
freed from all sins, is glorified in the heavenly world. / In the Kṛta age they praise asceticism, and in the Tretā age, knowledge;
in the Dvāpara age they say sacrifice, but in the Kali age gift alone. / Of all gifts whatsoever, this alone is the highest:
there is no gift higher than the protection given to all living beings. / But giving is paramount for a Śūdra, as the blessed Lord said.
Through giving, the attainment of all desires comes to him; it is his asceticism. / It is meritorious, purifying, prolonging life, and the destroyer of all sins.
This Purāṇa has been spoken, celebrating sacred places and śrāddhas. / The man who hears or reads it becomes prosperous.
Freed from all sins, he attains Hari together with Lakṣmī. / This has been spoken to you, O great king, meritorious and destructive of great sins,
and well worshiped by Brahmā, Arka, and the Rudras; those who know it proclaim that this must be heard. / This Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa has been proclaimed by me to you, O king,

the beginning of the Purāṇa, the ninefold creation at Puṣkara. / The wise man who recites it to Brahmins, and whoever hears or reads it, / rejoices in the world of Brahmā for a full hundred crore kalpas.

The Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa is complete. / May there be auspiciousness.

2.0.s: atha śrīpādme mahāpurāṇe dvitīyaṃ bhūmikhaṇḍaṃ prārabhyate
2.0.d: अथ श्रीपाद्मे महापुराणे द्वितीयं भूमिखण्डं प्रारभ्यते
2.0.m: Now begins the second section, the Bhūmikhaṇḍa, in the glorious Padma Mahāpurāṇa.

2.1.m: — Homage to glorious Gaṇeśa. / The sages said: Listen, O Sūta, most fortunate one, skilled in the meaning of all principles: / a terrible doubt has arisen, O wise one, destroying understanding.
Some recite about Prahlāda in the Purāṇas, O best of the twice-born: / though endowed with only five years, Keśava was pleased [by him].
When the war between gods and demons came about, how does he fight with Hari? / Slain by Vāsudeva, he entered the Vaiṣṇava body.
Sūta said: In ancient times it was known by Kaśyapa, and composed by the wise Vyāsa; / it was spoken previously by Brahmā in the presence of Vyāsa himself, the lord.
I shall declare that very thing before you, O twice-born; / the cause of the doubt that arose has been severed by the god, the Creator.
Vyāsa said: / Listen, O highly fortunate Sūta, to what was spoken by Brahmā / regarding the birth of Prahlāda, which is also heard differently in the Purāṇa.
As soon as he was born, bringing all happiness, he resorted to the Vaiṣṇava path; / foremost of the great Bhāgavatas, Prahlāda was worshipped by the gods.
To fight with Viṣṇu, he went into battle with his sons; / slain by Vāsudeva, he entered the Vaiṣṇava body.
Listen to the origin and nature of this great-souled one; / having entered battle with his sons and others against Viṣṇu, that valorous one,
entered the Vaiṣṇava splendor, having attained it by his own splendor. / How that valorous one was born in a former kalpa, O fortunate one,
the story of that hero I shall tell in brief. / In the west, on the shore of the ocean, there was indeed a city named Dvārakā,
endowed with all prosperity, possessed of all attainments. / In it always dwells a god-like man who knows yoga, the foremost knower of yoga,
renowned as Śivaśarman, skilled in the meaning of the Vedas and scriptures. / He too had five sons, skilled in the scriptures:
Yajñaśarman, Vedaśarman, and likewise Dharmaśarman, / and the fortunate Viṣṇuśarman, truly skilled in those duties.
The fifth was named Somaśarmā, entirely devoted to devotion to his father. / O best of the twice-born, apart from devotion to their father, no other dharma
did those great-souled ones know, imbued as they were with that feeling. / But Śivaśarmā, the best of the twice-born, seeing their devotion,
the wise one reflected: "I shall surpass even the best of the gods! / Whatever feeling there is among those devoted to their father—is that not established in their minds?
As I understand, so shall I act deliberately." / And indeed, by the grace of Viṣṇu, he had attained all magical powers.
O best of the twice-born, he contemplated an expedient to reveal their true nature; / indeed, through the power of his ascetic heat, that best of brahmins,
the foremost knower of Brahman, produced an illusion through his power. / Then, before them, Śivaśarmā displayed a deceptive appearance:
their mother was shown dead from a severe fever. / Seeing their mother dead, they spoke these words to their father:
"She by whom we were nurtured in the womb, O noble one, / has abandoned her body and gone of her own accord to destruction.
Having abandoned [us], she has gone to heaven, father; what is to be said?" / Śivaśarmā, [calling] his son devoted to devotion,
summoning Yajñaśarmā, the best of the twice-born said: / Śivaśarmā said: / "With this exceedingly sharp and whetted blade,
cut off all her limbs and throw them here and there!" / That was done by the son, exactly as the father's command was heard.
Returning thereafter, he spoke these words to his father: / "Just as you ordered, father, all that has been done by me.
Command me now with another task and purpose today; / and all of that, even if difficult to conquer or hard to achieve, I will do, O father!"
Recognizing that noble one as devoted to his father, the twice-born, / having known his supreme resolve, contemplated the second [son].
Summoning Vedaśarmā, [he said]: "Go at my command! / Without a woman, deluded by Love, I cannot survive.
By illusion, a woman endowed with all good fortune was displayed [by him]: / 'Bring this woman, my child, for my sake, with your resolve made firm.'"
Thus addressed, he replied: "I shall do what pleases you greatly." / Having bowed to his father, he went there and spoke to her:
"O lady, my father, afflicted by the arrows of Love, begs for you. / Therefore, though he is afflicted with old age, be gracious and fair-faced!
Serve my father, O beautiful woman whose every limb is charming!" / Such [words] of Vedaśarmā were heard by that illusory woman.
The woman said: / "Never do I desire one afflicted by old age, / whose mouth is diseased with phlegm, who is currently seized by sickness,
who is decrepit and suffering—an encounter with that old man! / I wish to delight with you; I will do what pleases you greatly,
with you who are adorned with beauty, auspicious fortune, and jewel-like qualities, / endowed with divine marks, having a divine form and great splendor!
What will you do with an old father? Listen, O giver of honor! / Through the disposition of enjoying my body, you will obtain all that is hard to gain.
Whatever you wish, O brahmin, that I shall give, no doubt." / Hearing these grave words, unpleasant and full of sin,
Vedaśarmā said: / "Your speech is connected with adharma, improper, and mixed with sin! / Do not speak like this to me, O lady, sinless and devoted to my father!
I have come for my father's sake; I beseech you, O auspicious woman! / Nothing else should be said in this manner; serve my father!
Whatever you wish in the three worlds of moving and unmoving beings, O lady, / that I shall give, without a doubt, even greater than the sovereignty of the gods, O auspicious one!"
The woman said: / "If you are capable of giving me so much for the sake of your father, / then show me this very day the gods, with Indra and Maheśvara!
You are indeed capable of giving what is hard to attain at present. / What is your strength, O noble one? Show it yourself!"
Vedaśarmā said: / "Behold, behold my strength, O lady, and the power of my austerities! / Summoned by me, the best of the gods, headed by Indra, have arrived!"
They said to Vedaśarmā: "What shall we do, O best of the twice-born? / Whatever you wish in this manner, O brahmin, that we give without a doubt."
Vedaśarmā said: / "If the gods are pleased with me, if their faces are gracious, / let them grant pure devotion to the feet of my father!"
"So be it!" [said] all the gods, and departed just as they had come. / Seeing that, she said to him: "The power of your asceticism has been seen.
I have no need of gods. If you wish to give here, / so that you may take me for your elder's sake, do what pleases me:
Give your own head, O brahmin, cutting it off with your own hand!" / Vedaśarmā said: / "I am blessed today, and I am freed from the three debts!
I shall give my own head, O lady; take it, take it, O auspicious one!" / With a sharp, keen-edged weapon, that best of the twice-born,
having cut off his own head, gave it to her while smiling; / and bathed in blood, she took it and went to the sage.
The woman said: / "Sent for your sake by your son, Vedaśarmā, / receive this head, severed by him himself.
His head was given to me by him who is devoted to your fatherhood. / For your sake, O tiger among the twice-born, enjoy me in this manner!"
That daring deed of Vedaśarmā was seen by those brothers of his; / they were seized with trembling limbs, [looking] at one another:
"Our virtuous mother, established in dharma, has died through her steadfastness in truth; / and this noble, auspicious one has died for our father's sake.
Blessed is he! He has attained blessedness; what is auspicious has been done for our father's sake!" / Thus it was spoken among those brothers of meritorious conduct.
Hearing their words and knowing him to be entirely devoted, / and that the head had been cut off by his son Vedaśarmā,
he then said to Dharmaśarmā: "Take hold of this head!"

2.2.m: Sūta said: / Taking it then, that great-souled one went forth in haste. / Through devotion to his father, through austerities, and by the power of truth and uprightness,
Dharmaśarmā then pulled Dharma [himself] there. / Indeed, Dharma, drawn by the ascetic heat of that wise one,
came to Dharmaśarmā and spoke this word: / "Why have I been summoned by you, O Dharmaśarmā? I have arrived.
Tell me that purpose of yours; I shall accomplish it, without a doubt." / Dharmaśarmā said: / "If there is service to the elder, if there is devotion and unwavering asceticism,
by that truth, O Dharma, let my [brother] Vedaśarmā live!" / Dharma said: / "By your self-control, purity, truth, and austerities, O you of good vows,
and through devotion to your father, your mighty-armed brother Vedaśarmā, / that great-souled one, shall indeed regain his life.
I am pleased by this austerity and by devotion to your father, O highly wise one! / Choose a boon—blessing be upon you—one that is difficult even for the foremost knowers of dharma to attain!"
When that good speech was heard by him, Dharmaśarmā, / that one of great renown said to the great-souled Vaivasvata:
"Give me unwavering devotion to the worship of my father's feet, / delight in dharma, and liberation, if you are well pleased with me!"
Dharma then said to him: "By my grace it shall be so." / When that great statement was spoken, Vedaśarmā arose.
As if waking from sleep, the very wise one said to Dharmaśarman: / 'Where has that goddess gone, brother? Where might our father be?'
It was related in brief how he had been directed by his father. / Having understood it, Dharmaśarman, delighted, said to him:
'Today, O fortunate one, by my head and by my life, / turn your face toward me, brother; who else is like you on earth?'
Having spoken thus to his brother, eager to see their father, / he made up his mind to go together with his brother Dharmaśarman.
Those two, cheerful in mind, went there to their father; / approaching the excellent Śivaśarman there, the two of them,
Dharmaśarman then said to his radiant father: / 'Today, O fortunate one, by my ascetic power and my life,
Vedaśarman has been brought back; accept that son, sir!' / Śivaśarman was then delighted, recognizing his devotion,
yet he said nothing to him, but fell into thought again. / [Then,] looking at the noble-minded one standing before him with humility,
he addressed Viṣṇuśarman: 'My child, do my bidding: / go to Indra's realm today, and bring nectar from there.
I wish now to dwell together with this beloved woman. / That nectar which arose from the ocean destroys diseases.
She does not truly desire me; do that quickly / so that I may obtain her, otherwise she will go to another.
Knowing me to be old, this young and beautiful girl will despise me. / Today, together with this beloved goddess, in the three worlds,
so that I may become flawless and free of disease, O father, / do that for me, my child, since you are devoted to me on earth.'
Having heard that speech of his noble father, / Viṣṇuśarman then spoke to his father of blazing splendor:
'I will do all this to bring you the highest happiness.' / Having spoken thus, the righteous and noble-minded Viṣṇuśarman,
bowed down to his father and circumambulated him, / and by his great strength, ascetic power, and observance,
he went into the sky as he journeyed, the wise one; / with the speed of a great wind, he went directly toward Indra.

2.3.m: Sūta said: / As he set out by that path and entered the middle of the sky, / he was seen by the thousand-eyed wise god of gods.
Knowing his endeavor, the king of the gods created an obstacle. / He said this to Menakā: 'Go by my command;
go quickly, slender-waisted one, and cause an obstacle for him, / for this very best of brahmins, the son of Śivaśarman.
Act so—blessings unto you—that he does not come to my abode.' / Having heard his speech, Menakā set out in haste.
Sūta said: / Endowed with beauty and gracious qualities, adorned with every ornament, / she appeared upon a swing at the edge of the Nandana forest,
singing a song with a sweet voice resembling the sound of a lute. / She was seen by him, large-eyed, clever, and with lovely eyes.
Recognizing her design and her supreme obstacle, / [knowing that] she was sent by Indra and would bring no good,
knowing this, the best of twice-borns went on quickly. / Seen by her, he was asked: 'Where are you going, O noble-minded one?'
Viṣṇuśarman then said to Menakā, who moves at will: / 'I am going to Indra's realm in haste for the sake of my father.'
Menakā answered Viṣṇuśarman again with sweet words: / 'I am pierced by the arrows of love, and today have taken refuge with you.
Protect me, O tiger among twice-borns, if you desire dharma in this world. / The moment you were seen by me with a mind agitated by love,
I was utterly consumed by the fire of love, without a doubt. / Bewildered and tormented by desire, show me favor and turn your face to me!'
Viṣṇuśarman said: / 'The conduct of the god of gods is known to me, O fair-faced one; / and I know yours too; I am not such a one, auspicious lady.
Others are deluded by your splendor and charms, lovely lady, / Viśvāmitra and the rest, O goddess; I am the son of Śivaśarman.
Even when one has attained perfection in yoga and asceticism, O fragile woman, / love and other great flaws are conquered at the very outset.
Resort to another, large-eyed one; I am going to Indra's realm.' / Having spoken thus, the best of the twice-born went on swiftly.
Menakā, having failed, was questioned by the wielder of the thunderbolt. / He displayed terrifying sights of various forms again and again.
Just as heaps of grass burned by fire, O twice-borns, / turn into mere ashes, so too did those terrifying apparitions.
By the splendor of that brahmin devoted to his father, O best of men, / those dreadful, terrible terrors were dissolved, O twice-borns.
The thousand-eyed one displayed obstacles repeatedly; / the renowned brahmin destroyed them with his own splendor.
Thus the intelligent one destroyed many obstacles of that noble Indra, / by his asceticism and his splendor.
When those terrible and mighty obstacles had been destroyed, / knowing the fierce obstacles of dreadful form made by him,
then the best of twice-borns, Viṣṇuśarman of great splendor, grew angry; / the illustrious one, his eyes reddened at the corners with wrath toward Indra, [thought:]
'I will cast Indra down from Indra's realm, not otherwise! / Whoever creates an obstacle today for one devoted to his own duty,
to him I will give punishment: he who strikes shall indeed be struck down! / Thus I will make another the guardian of the gods.'
As the best of brahmins was thus preparing to destroy Indra, / just then the lord of gods, the subduer of Pāka, arrived.
'Hail, O highly wise brahmin! In asceticism, observance, / self-control, truth, and purity, there is no other equal to you.
By this devotion to your father, I, along with the gods, have been conquered. / You ought to forgive all my offense, O best of men.
Choose a boon—blessings unto you—and I will grant what is hard to obtain.' / Viṣṇuśarman then spoke to the king of gods who had come in that manner:
'The power of a brahmin, O lord of great Indra, is unbearable to gods and deities; / the power of one devoted to his father, O lord of gods, is wholly insupportable, O almighty one.
Destruction of the splendor of noble brahmins must not be done. / Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, together with all their sons and grandsons,
would be destroyed, without doubt, if the best of twice-borns are angered. / If you had not come today, then your supreme sovereignty,
by the power of my own asceticism, with eyes full of anger, / I had become desirous of giving to another noble soul.
You have come here today, desiring to give a boon: / give me nectar, O lord of gods, and unswerving devotion to my father.
Grant such a boon if you are pleased, O slayer of foes.' / [Indra said:] 'I grant you such a meritorious boon, along with the nectar.'
Having spoken thus to that brahmin, he himself gave the nectar; / he gave it along with a jar to him, with a delighted soul, [saying:]
'May your devotion to your father be unswerving forever, O twice-born.' / Having addressed the brahmin thus, the thousand-eyed one took his leave,
and became pleased, having seen that insupportable power of the brahmin. / Viṣṇuśarman then went and spoke words to his father.
"Father, I have brought from Indra the nectar that destroys disease. / By this, O fortunate one, become free from sickness forever!
Attain highest satisfaction this very day through this nectar!" / Having heard these weighty words of his son, Śivaśarman
summoned all his sons with a delighted heart [and said]: / "You sons are devoted to your father, obedient to my word.
Choose a boon, O children, well pleased, [a boon] rare in the world!" / Thus spoken to, they, all in agreement, listened to him.
After consulting together, they replied to their father: / "While we are alive, our mother has gone to the abode of Yama.
May the virtuous lady return from that abode free from sickness by your favor! / May you be our father and she our mother in birth after birth, O father,
and may all of us be your sons, doers of meritorious deeds!" / Śivaśarman said: "Though she died this very day, your mother, affectionate to her sons,
shall come back alive and very joyful; of this there is no doubt." / When this auspicious word was spoken by the sage Śivaśarman,
their mother arrived, overjoyed, and spoke these words: / "For this purpose is a son, born of good seed, brought into the world;
men desire a virtuous son who adds glory to the family and lineage. / In this world, women who are fortunate, exceedingly meritorious, and fond of merit
desire a son everywhere—one of pure body, an achiever of merit. / She into whose womb enters and abides an exceedingly meritorious embryo,
that woman, sharing in merit, gives birth to meritorious sons / who preserve family conduct, uphold the family, and deliver their father and mother.
Without merits, how can a woman obtain an excellent son? / I do not know by what merits this highly meritorious husband,
born with the power of dharma, righteous and fond of dharma, [was gained], / by whose seed I have obtained you, sons even greater than he!
Such is the power of merit! You, affectionate toward merit, / have become my sons, utterly dedicated to father-devotion.
Ah, in the worlds a virtuous son is obtained by merits! / Five high-souled [sons], each superior to the next, have been obtained by me—
sacrificers of virtuous character, endowed with austerity, splendor, and valor." / Thus praised repeatedly by their mother,
the sons, filled with great joy, bowed to their mother. / The sons said: "By supreme merits a mother, a good mother, and a good father are obtained indeed.
You, a merit-making mother, were granted to us by our fortunes; / having entered your womb, we have grown through supreme merits.
In birth after birth may you be our mother and he our father!" / The father said: "Listen, my sons, to an excellent boon that bestows merit:
When I am pleased, let my sons enjoy imperishable pleasures." / The sons said: "If, father, you are pleased and wish to give a boon here,
send us to Goloka, the Vaiṣṇava realm free from torment!" / The father said: "Go to the Vaiṣṇava realm, you who are freed from sin,
by my favor, by your austerities, and by this devotion to your father of yours!" / When this auspicious speech was spoken by that sage,
he who holds the conch, discus, and mace in hand arrived, mounted upon Garuḍa. / To Śivaśarman, together with his sons, he spoke thus again and again:
"Today, O twice-born, I have been conquered through devotion by you together with your sons! / Come along with your four sons who perform meritorious deeds,
along with this virtuous wife who desires her husband!" / Śivaśarman said: "Let these sons of mine go to the supreme Vaiṣṇava realm;
I, however, shall spend some time on earth with my wife / and with this good son, the youngest, Somaśarman."
When this auspicious word was spoken by the truth-speaking sage, / the Lord of the gods then addressed those virtuous sons of Śivaśarman:
"Let them go to the realm that bestows liberation, free from torment and dissolution!" / When this was spoken, those four twice-born men of truthful heart
all assumed the form of Viṣṇu that very instant; / with complexions like lapis lazuli, bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
endowed with the fortune of all ornaments, having the form of Viṣṇu, possessing great splendor, / adorned with necklaces and bracelets, beautified with gem garlands,
resembling the brilliance of the sun, enveloped in blazing splendor, / entered the body of Viṣṇu before the eyes of Śivaśarman.
Just as flames merge into a flame, so they merged, O wise one! / Those best of the twice-born went to the Vaiṣṇava abode through father-devotion.
I shall now proclaim the true power of Somaśarman.
